The VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) lost 1%, led by declines in Micron Technology , Advanced Micro Devices and Sandisk . Semiconductors have struggled this week amid jitters about competition from China . The SMH is down 8% week to date, on pace for its biggest weekly decline since July. The tech-heavy index was on track for its worst week since April 2025 . The Dow, on the other hand, has moved higher by less than 1% on the week. Investors have also grown concerned that tech companies are borrowing too much for the AI buildout . Shares of neoclouds like CoreWeave , which has seen its total debt rise to more than $51 billion , were down 10%, putting the stock's week-to-date losses at more than 23%. "The question is: Is this a systemic issue?" said Michael Rosen, Angeles' chief investment officer. "Obviously, increased debt issuance is something to observe and continue to watch and be concerned about if it continues to get to levels of excessiveness. But we're not remotely close to that right now." Other areas of the market such as energy saw gains Friday, with stocks like Chevron helping to keep the Dow's losses in check. That's as oil prices moved higher amid rising tensions between the U.S. and Iran as well as between Russian and Ukraine. West Texas Intermediate crude futures increased 3.51% to settle at $101.41 per barrel, while Brent crude futures advanced 3.72% to $109.86. Simultaneously, investors have been grappling with hotter-than-expected inflation data, which has been exacerbated by elevated energy prices in the wake of the U.S.-Iran war. Wholesale inflation this week saw its biggest gain since 2022 , while consumer inflation remained well above the Federal Reserve's target of 2%. Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh spoke at an IMF event in Bangkok overnight. And while he didn't comment on whether the Fed would raise rates before year-end, traders took that as a sign that the central bank will hold policy steady later this month. The CME Group's FedWatch tool points to an 85% chance the Fed keeps its overnight rate unchanged at its Oct. 27-28 meeting. The index last closed above that level on July 29 , when markets fell after the Federal Reserve kept interest rates steady at its meeting that month. headlines.article_text: Netflix hires Peter Rice to run content. Here's what it means Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Netflix has replaced its chief content officer, Bela Bajaria, with former Disney executive Peter Rice. Rice brings a wealth of experience in television and film, including scripted and unscripted shows, live sports telecasts, prestige television and theatrical distribution. Netflix's viewership has stagnated in recent quarters. It reports quarterly earnings on Tuesday. In this article NFLX Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Peter Rice, seen here on May 3, 2017, was head of Disney's TV entertainment business in 2020. He was one of several executives passed over for the CEO job in favor of Chapek. David Paul Morris | Bloomberg | Getty Images Netflix is shaking up its C-suite in an effort to fix its engagement woes. On Thursday, the streaming giant announced that former Disney executive Peter Rice will take over as the company's chief content officer, overseeing global content organization, including scripted and unscripted series, film and live events. Rice is replacing 10-year Netflix veteran Bela Bajaria , who most recently led the company's global content team with a focus on its live sports strategy . Bajaria was initially hired in 2016 to help the streamer launch an unscripted division as well as licensing and studio co-productions. She later transitioned to the top creative role, spearheading Netflix's $20 billion content budget. She oversaw popular TV series like "Stranger Things," "Wednesday," "Bridgerton," "Squid Game," "Adolescence" and "Beef," as well as Netflix films like "Frankenstein" and "KPop Demon Hunters." Bajaria also helped push Netflix into live sports and events, including deals with the WWE and the NFL as well as programs like "The Roast of Tom Brady." Prior to his stint at Disney, Rice was president of 21st Century Fox and CEO of Fox Networks Group as well as Fox's lead executive on the Hulu board. He was also the president of Fox Searchlight Pictures and helped release "Slumdog Millionaire," "Juno," "Little Miss Sunshine" and "Sideways." The executive change follows a tumultuous period for Netflix as it faces stagnating viewership and explores avenues for growth. It comes just days after the streaming giant laid off roughly 1,000 employees , or 6% of its workforce. The last time Netflix made cuts of this size was in 2022 when it reported its first quarterly subscriber loss in more than 10 years. "We believe this round of layoffs reflects more structural changes to the cost base than a reaction to near-term subscriber dynamics," wrote Brian Pitz, managing director and head of internet and interactive entertainment equity research at BMO Capital Markets, in a research note published Friday. Flagging engagement In July, Netflix reported viewership increased just 2% in the first half of the year as the streamer suffers from a lack of shows with water-cooler-level hype. Co-CEO Ted Sarandos admitted last month during the Bloomberg Screentime conference that the company is "not growing as fast as I want us to." Those warnings, and now Bajaria's exit, have Wall Street bracing for more turbulence ahead. "The sudden departure of Bajaria likely signals to us that user engagement may have remained soft throughout [the third quarter]," Pitz wrote. Netflix is set to release fiscal third-quarter earnings on Tuesday. In July, Nielsen reported that Netflix had generated 7.8% of TV viewership, while YouTube accounted for nearly double that, at 14.2%. YouTube has been Netflix's biggest threat in the battle for viewers' time. In response, the streaming giant has sought to diversify its content in recent years, expanding into live sports, documentaries and video games in order to compete for share of consumer attention. "If the opportunity is to recast [Netflix] into a broader content hub, the risk is missing the watercooler originals," Steven Cahall, equity analyst at Wells Fargo, wrote in a research note last month. "We see breakout hits as a must for the stock to work again." What Rice brings to Netflix Rice has a wealth of experience in television and film, most recently serving as the chairman of Walt Disney Television and chairman of general entertainment for the company. He managed a wide swath of channels across broadcast and streaming, including ABC, Disney Channel, Hulu and FX Networks. During his tenure, he oversaw the production of more than 300 shows, including "American Idol," "Modern Family," "Abbott Elementary," "The Bear," "Only Murders in the Building" and "Shogun." He also headed up major sporting events such as coverage of the Super Bowl, NBA Finals and FIFA World Cup. Under Rice's leadership, Disney earned roughly 300 Primetime Emmy nominations between 2021 and 2022. Of those nods, it won nearly 60 awards across its television networks and streaming platforms. Meanwhile, Netflix's Emmy wins have slowed. In 2021, it tied the record for most trophies won by an outlet in a single year with 44. This year, however, it only took home 16 prizes, its lowest Emmy haul in a decade. With Rice, Netflix is also getting an executive with theatrical experience. After he was ousted by then-Disney CEO Bob Chapek in mid-2022, he transitioned into an independent producer role. Since 2023 he has produced films like "Saturday Night" and "28 Years Later." He's currently developing a movie adaptation of the video game "Elden Ring." Late last year, Netflix struck a deal to buy Warner Bros. Discovery's film studio and streaming assets, only to be outbid months later by Paramount Skydance, which completed its acquisition of WBD in early October. Some on Wall Street have speculated that the streamer may be interested in further M&A, including acquiring assets from NBCUniversal after it splits from parent company Comcast . "[Rice's] long tenure at Fox, and then Disney after its acquisition of Fox, gives him unique insight into the consolidation of two major studios, relevant if Netflix chooses to go after another studio," Alicia Reese, senior vice president of equity research at Wedbush, wrote in a research note Thursday. "Even if it doesn't, Rice's experience fits well as Netflix pushes deeper into theatrical and builds a broader platform with varied content across the entertainment ecosystem." headlines.title: Apple’s $1,999 iPhone Duo puts the company's status-symbol power to the test
headlines.summary: Apple’s $1,999 iPhone Duo is drawing early demand as analysts assess whether the foldable can lift iPhone pricing and revenue.
headlines.article_text: Apple iPhone Duo demand, pricing and revenue impact Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Apple's iPhone Duo launch-day pickup inventory sold out quickly, with some delivery estimates already slipping into late January online. The first foldable iPhone reaches $3,199 at 2TB, creating a new tier above the Pro and Pro Max. Analysts say the Duo could boost Apple’s average selling prices through trade-ups, Android switchers, and a halo effect across the rest of the iPhone lineup. In this article AAPL Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 2:19 02:19 First impressions of the iPhone Duo — Apple's biggest iPhone redesign ever News Videos Apple 's iPhone Duo , its most expensive iPhone ever, went up for preorder Friday, with launch-day pickup inventory selling out and some online delivery estimates already slipping into late January. The company said in a statement that the pre-order demand was "nothing short of extraordinary." "We are working hard to get this revolutionary new product into customers' hands as quickly as possible, and we will continue accepting orders online," Apple said. Apple's first foldable phone starts at $1,999 and passes $3,000 at the 2TB storage tier. It is the biggest change to the physical design of the iPhone in years and establishes an entirely new price point above the Pro and Pro Max. The early rush offers a first glimpse at the demand behind Apple's bet: Whether a dramatic new design can persuade customers to spend more and push the iPhone even further as a status symbol. But analysts who spoke with CNBC said Apple's bet is not that foldables suddenly become a mass-market product. It is that a relatively small group of its highest-spending customers can become significantly more valuable. Foldables are expected to make up just over 2% of global smartphone units this year but nearly 7% of industry revenue, according to IDC. By 2030, IDC expects the category to account for 10% of smartphone revenue while still representing only about 3% of units. That gap between volume and value is central to Apple's opportunity. "Duo is fast becoming an aspirational foldable," IDC's Nabila Popal told CNBC, comparing its appeal with Apple's broader position as an aspirational smartphone brand. Apple CEO John Ternus, alongside vice president of industrial design Molly Anderson, shows off the new iPhone Duo during an Apple event at the Steve Jobs Theater in Apple Park in Cupertino, California, on September 9, 2026. Karl Mondon | Afp | Getty Images Popal, global senior research director for the Consumer Device Team at IDC, said the technology itself is not necessarily the breakthrough. Foldable Android phones have existed for years. What's new is Apple bringing that form factor to the enormous base of consumers already invested in the iPhone ecosystem. Apple itself has been exploring the form factor for more than a decade. In 2011, Ternus and five other Apple engineers filed a patent application for foldable electronic devices, according to a recent TIME profile. "It's not that it's a breakthrough or new technology, but it's from Apple," Popal said. The Duo could also prove more accessible than some industry watchers had anticipated. Anshel Sag, an analyst at Moor Insights who attended Apple's launch event, said many expected the foldable iPhone to start between $2,400 and $2,500. Apple coming in at $1,999, Sag said, suggests the company "wants a lot of share." Sag expects the Duo to become "very much a status symbol" during the holiday season and potentially into next year. That status appeal could be reinforced by scarcity. Apple has an installed base of roughly 1.4 billion iPhones, he noted, meaning even a small percentage of early adopters could overwhelm the roughly 6 million or fewer units Counterpoint expects to be available near term. IDC also expects supply to be constrained initially because of the complexity of the device and Apple's manufacturing and quality standards. "Exclusivity is part of the current appeal," Popal said. And Apple has made explicit luxury plays before. When the first Apple Watch launched, the company offered an 18-karat gold Edition starting at $10,000. Apple also formed a long-running partnership with Hermès around premium watch bands and designs. That push came during the tenure of Angela Ahrendts, the former Burberry CEO who joined Apple in 2014 to lead retail and online stores, as the company experimented with bringing more of the language and presentation of luxury fashion into its stores and products. The Duo takes that idea into Apple's largest product business. Low volume, high value IDC expects Apple to ship roughly 7 million units this year, or roughly 3% of Apple's total shipments in 2026. Popal, the IDC analyst, forecasts Duo shipments could grow another 70% next year. That would give Apple roughly 40% of the global foldable market and would make it the category's largest player, surpassing Samsung and Huawei. According to her forecast, Apple could ship as many Duos in the next six months as the previous category leaders did in all of 2025. But the more important number for Apple may not be units. A large share of Duo customers are expected to be existing iPhone owners, analysts said, including consumers who otherwise might have purchased a Pro Max and are now trading up to a device costing hundreds of dollars more. Others could add the Duo as a second smartphone, with Apple's ecosystem allowing users to move relatively seamlessly between it and their primary iPhone. The bank expects the Duo to have a disproportionate impact on iPhone revenue because of its much higher average selling price, even as overall iPhone shipments are expected to remain roughly flat next year. Davidson analyst Gil Luria said Apple needs the Duo to succeed as it comes up against a difficult set of earnings comps with its strongest upgrade cycle in years. "Without an uplift from Duo, they may experience some pretty pedestrian revenue growth," Luria told CNBC. The device gives Apple several ways to generate that uplift, he added. It raises the company's average selling price by capturing die-hard Apple customers who might otherwise have bought a Pro Max. It could bring in some consumers who previously bought folding Android phones because Apple did not offer one. And it could create a halo around the rest of the iPhone lineup. Luria said some consumers will visit Apple stores specifically to see the Duo, "but probably walk out with an iPhone or iPhone Pro at half the price." That means the Duo can potentially help Apple even when someone decides not to buy it. Lead times for the iPhone 18 Pro have softened in several markets compared with the prior cycle, while the more expensive Pro Max has held up better, according to JPMorgan's tracking. Andrew Harnik | Getty Images President Donald Trump on Friday denied that the White House had ordered restrictions this week on Starlink satellite internet services provided to Ukraine's armed forces. Ukrainian officials on Tuesday and Wednesday said SpaceX had restricted use of Starshield, a military-grade version of Starlink, without warning, impeding some military operations and its ability to defend civilians against intensifying attacks by Russia. Musk pinned responsibility for any restrictions on the U.S. government and President Trump, writing on X that, "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government." Reporters in Washington, D.C., on Friday asked Trump who was responsible for pausing access for the Ukrainian military. "Well, I don't know if it was anybody because it wasn't me, and I don't think it was Elon," Trump said. "And from what I understand, it's the same as it's always been." Ukrainian forces have long relied on Starlink and Starshield to enable data gathering by their autonomous drones and for other communications. The restrictions cut off connectivity for drones or other vehicles traveling above 160 kilometers per hour. Serhii Beskrestnov, an advisor to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, wrote in a post on Telegram this week that, "Our armed forces did not receive a warning about these restrictions, and this led to the failure of a number of missions." Radoslaw Sikorski, Poland's deputy prime minister, criticized Musk on X about the restrictions. Poland has purchased Starlink services for Ukraine from SpaceX. "Hey, @elonmusk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again?" he wrote . "As your European customers, we are watching you." Musk is an advisor to the Pentagon on technology through his role in the recently announced Project Meridian. Musk and SpaceX did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Friday. headlines.summary: The U.S. raised market access issues for Mastercard and Citigroup in China during bilateral meetings in Bangkok this week, a U.S. Treasury official says.
headlines.article_text: U.S. raises Mastercard, Citigroup China market access in talks: Official Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points U.S. officials raised market access issues for Mastercard and Citigroup in China during bilateral meetings in Bangkok this week, according to a U.S. Treasury official. The regulatory approval was agreed to during Chinese leader Xi’s September Washington visit with President Trump, the official said. The progress follows China's Oct. 13 approval for Visa to begin preparing a wholly owned domestic card-clearing business. In this article MA C Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT A Citibank branch in New York, US, on Sunday, Oct. 11, 2026. Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty Images BANGKOK – U.S. officials pressed Beijing on market access issues for Mastercard Inc and Citigroup Inc during at least two bilateral meetings with Chinese counterparts in Bangkok this week, according to a U.S. Treasury official. The Treasury delegation, led by Deputy Secretary Francis Brooke, held bilateral meetings with officials from the People's Bank of China and the finance ministry on the sidelines of the Group of 20 finance meetings and the IMF-World Bank annual gathering this week, the official said, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss the closed-door meetings. The talks included market access for U.S. companies, including Mastercard, Visa and Citigroup, the official said, adding that regulatory approval was part of the agreement reached during the meeting between Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping during the latter's state visit in Washington last month. The sideline meetings in Bangkok continued discussions on implementing these deals, the official said. The PBOC, China's National Financial Regulatory Administration, China Securities Regulatory Commission, Chinese embassies in Singapore and Thailand, the U.S. Treasury Department press office and Visa did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment. Citigroup and Mastercard declined to comment. The progress follows China's Oct. 13 approval for Visa Inc. to begin preparing a wholly owned domestic card-clearing business . Visa has up to a year to prepare before it applies for an operating license, the PBOC has said . China has opened much of its financial sector to foreign firms since 2018, gradually lifting foreign ownership caps on services such as securities, futures and fund management. It still limits cross-border capital flows and has kept state-backed domestic players dominant in payments. Mastercard currently operates yuan card payments in China through a local joint venture with NetsUnion Clearing Corp., which began operating in 2024. The pending approval would allow it to operate as an independent entity, the person said. Citigroup — which has hired several dozen employees for its China unit — is seeking a wholly owned securities license to conduct A-share brokerage, underwriting, research and principal trading businesses in the onshore market, two people familiar with the industry said, requesting anonymity for discussing private matters. One of the two people close to Citigroup said the bank planned to increase its China securities staff to about 100. The bank applied in late 2021, and Reuters reported last month that approval could come soon. Trump and Xi are expected to meet in person for the third time this year in Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in November. "The move suggests the US-China trade environment remains benign, and Beijing is keen to keep up the momentum," said Dan Wang, China director at Eurasia Group. Licensing U.S. financial firms is a "limited concession" on market access, she said, though it signals China is continuing to open up, and "this should marginally bolster investor confidence in Chinese assets."
